name: Do Not Track
plain: Header and property saying the person asked not to be tracked; mostly ignored.
meaning: Reveals a privacy preference (about 1 in 4 desktop Chrome and Firefox users enabled it at its peak) and ironically adds a fingerprint bit. Safari removed it in 12.1; Firefox is removing the setting.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

limits.headline: Can see whether you turned on Do Not Track, which most sites ignore
limits.user_action: Nothing. Your browser sends it with each page request if the setting is on
can: Check if you asked not to be tracked
Use the setting as one more clue to recognise your browser
cannot: Make sites stop tracking you; most do not honor it
See the setting in Safari, which removed it
Know why you turned it on
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Firefox still send it if you turn it on. Safari removed it.

story.what_it_is: A setting that tells sites you do not want to be tracked, which most ignore.

marketing.name: Do Not Track
marketing.pitch: Mozilla describes a browser setting that asks sites not to track you, and notes that sites choose whether to respond.

story.for_you: If you turn it on, every site gets a small note saying 'please do not track me'. You see no change. Most sites ignore it, and having it on can make your browser stand out.
story.for_makers: Few makers honor it, because there is no law that requires it. Some analytics tools skip counting those visits. It is also a fingerprint bit, since only some people turn it on.

use_cases.example: A privacy minded analytics tool skips counting visits that carry the request.
An ad network reads the flag and keeps tracking, since no rule forces them to stop.
A news site shows a 'we do not respond to this' note in its privacy policy.
A game site that tracks play time for ads ignores the request, because it is not required to follow it.
A fingerprinting script adds the flag as one more clue to tell visitors apart.
A store records the preference but still uses cookies for the cart.

technical_bounds: No legal force; replaced by GPC

linkedin.how: Do Not Track read but excluded from hash. Read by the LinkedIn APFC fingerprint script (alleged by BrowserGate, partly confirmed by BleepingComputer).
